newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany not ready for EMU top institute says.
newsitem.headline: Germany not ready for EMU top institute says.

text.p: Germany's government deficit will exceed the Maastricht Treaty deficit and debt criteria this year, Udo Ludwig, chief economist of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, said on Monday.
Ludwig told Reuters Financial Television: "Germany will run up a government deficit of between three and 3.5 percent of GDP this year and the debt will be slightly higher than 60 percent of GDP."

The reference values for EU states to take part in the single European Currency (EMU) are three percent for government deficit and 60 percent for government debt in relation to GDP. Ability to join EMU in 1999 will be judged on the 1997 data.
Ludwig is convinced, however, that the common currency will be launched on time anyway. "The treaty provides sufficient room for a flexible interpretation of the criteria," Ludwig said.
He added that this did not necessarily mean that countries like Italy and Spain which are far off the crucial reference values will have to be admitted as well.

With regard to Germany's economic growth rate the Halle institute also maintains a pessimistic view. "We expect a GDP growth of about two or 2.1 percent only," Ludwig said, adding, "This won't even be enough to stop the rise of unemployment, let alone bring down joblessness."

The positive upshot of those forecasts is a continuing low interest rate level. Ludwig does not see any danger on the inflation front and thus believes that the Bundesbank will not move rates during the next half year.

In addition, Ludwig is convinced that even money supply growth above the Bundesbank's target range of 3.5 percent to 6.5 percent will not worry the central bank. "I don't think that the Bundesbank will meet its target this year, but it won't react to this by raising interest rates," Ludwig said.
